text: [Stripe] Stripe's pricing looks simple, but disputes cost $15 each and the fee is not refunded even if you win. For a low-margin shop that adds up fast, so I would not pick it for high-chargeback products.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Many founders report that Stripe froze their account with little warning and held funds for weeks. Support replies are mostly templated, which makes it a risky single point of failure for a young business.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Stripe is powerful, but it is built for developers. If nobody on your team can maintain webhooks and tax logic, you will spend more time on plumbing than on selling, and a simpler tool fits better.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] For EU digital goods, Stripe leaves VAT registration and filing to you. Stripe Tax calculates the amount, but you still own the compliance work, which is a real gap for solo sellers.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] I'd be cautious with Stripe if you sell in many countries. Payout currencies, cross-border fees and extra FX charges make the real cost noticeably higher than the headline 2.9% + 30c.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Stripe tends to flag businesses it considers high risk, such as supplements, CBD or crypto. Approval can be revoked later, so it is a poor base for those niches.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Migrating away from Stripe is painful. Stored cards live in its vault, and exporting them needs a manual PCI-compliant transfer, so lock-in is a genuine downside to weigh up front.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Stripe Billing gets complicated quickly: proration, trials and usage meters each need custom handling. Teams often outgrow its defaults and end up with brittle glue code.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Honestly, Stripe isn't a good match for marketplaces with large payouts. Connect fees stack on top of processing fees, and onboarding sellers adds friction that competitors handle better.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Users on forums often say Stripe's phone support is basically non-existent. When a payment issue hits production, you may wait days for an answer, which is hard to accept for a payments vendor.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Paddle's 5% + 50c fee is steep for small tickets. On a $10 product you lose about 10%, so unless you really need the merchant-of-record service, it is an expensive choice.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Because Paddle is the merchant of record, you do not own the customer relationship. Refund rules, invoices and branding follow Paddle's terms, which can frustrate teams that want control.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Paddle's approval process is strict and slow. Several sellers describe being rejected without a clear reason, and appeals take weeks, so don't build a launch plan around it.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Payouts from Paddle follow a fixed schedule with a delay, and funds can be held during reviews. Cash flow is harder to predict than with a direct processor.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Paddle's checkout customisation is limited compared with Stripe. If conversion tuning matters to you, the overlay checkout and fixed flows will feel restrictive.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] I wouldn't recommend Paddle for physical goods or marketplaces. It focuses on software, so unsupported categories get declined, and the platform offers few workarounds.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Reporting in Paddle is weaker than expected: exports are basic, and reconciling payouts with your own books takes manual work. Finance teams often complain about this.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] Paddle has changed its pricing and policies several times, and some customers say the updates came with little notice. That unpredictability is a concern for long-term planning.
label: negative

text: [PayPal] PayPal is known for holding funds for up to 180 days after a dispute. Sellers regularly describe this as stressful, and the buyer-favouring policy makes it a weak option for merchants.
label: negative

text: [PayPal] PayPal's developer experience is inconsistent: legacy NVP, REST v1 and v2 endpoints coexist, and the docs contradict each other. Integration takes much longer than it should.
label: negative

text: [PayPal] Account limitations on PayPal can appear suddenly and are hard to reverse. Support is slow, so relying on it as your only payment method is risky.
label: negative

text: [PayPal] PayPal's fees for international and currency-converted payments are high, and the conversion spread is rarely shown upfront. I'd avoid it for cross-border subscriptions.
label: negative

text: [PayPal] Recurring billing on PayPal feels clunky. Failed payments are retried in ways you cannot fully control, and customers must have a PayPal login, which hurts conversion.
label: negative

text: [Adyen] Adyen is aimed at large enterprises. Minimum volumes and a long sales process make it a poor fit for startups, and smaller merchants get little attention from the team.
label: negative

text: [Adyen] Getting started with Adyen takes weeks of onboarding and contract talks. For a small SaaS that needs to launch quickly, that overhead is hard to justify.
label: negative

text: [Adyen] Adyen's documentation is thorough but dense, and its pricing is quote-based, so you cannot easily compare it with competitors. Many teams find the lack of transparency off-putting.
label: negative

text: [Adyen] Reports suggest Adyen's support is geared to key accounts. Smaller merchants wait longer for answers, which becomes a problem when a settlement issue appears.
label: negative

text: [Braintree] Braintree has seen little product investment since the PayPal acquisition. New features are slow to arrive, and many developers now see it as a legacy choice.
label: negative

text: [Braintree] Braintree's dispute handling is manual, and the dashboard feels dated. For a team that wants modern tooling, Stripe or Adyen is a stronger option.
label: negative

text: [Braintree] Support quality at Braintree is uneven. Several merchants mention long delays and being redirected to PayPal teams, which doesn't inspire confidence for critical payment flows.
label: negative

text: [Square] Square works well in person, but its online tools are limited. Subscriptions, international sales and custom checkout are weak points, so it is not ideal for a SaaS.
label: negative

text: [Square] Square has a reputation for sudden account holds and terminations, especially after unusually large transactions. Business owners often say the explanations are vague.
label: negative

text: [Square] Outside the US, Canada, the UK, Australia and a few other markets, Square is unavailable. That makes it a non-starter for companies selling globally.
label: negative

text: [Lemon Squeezy] Since the Stripe acquisition, Lemon Squeezy's roadmap has felt uncertain. Updates have slowed and support responses lag, so I'd hesitate to depend on it for a growing business.
label: negative

text: [Lemon Squeezy] Lemon Squeezy takes a 5% + 50c cut and offers fewer integrations than larger platforms. Sellers who outgrow it find that moving subscribers elsewhere is awkward.
label: negative

text: [Lemon Squeezy] Payout delays and account reviews are a frequent complaint about Lemon Squeezy. Merchants with tight cash flow may find the unpredictability difficult.
label: negative

text: [Lemon Squeezy] Lemon Squeezy's analytics and tax reporting are basic. If you need detailed revenue breakdowns, you will have to export data and build the reports yourself.
label: negative

text: [FastSpring] FastSpring's interface feels outdated, and the setup process leans heavily on its sales team. Self-serve developers often find it slower and more rigid than modern alternatives.
label: negative

text: [FastSpring] FastSpring is rarely cheap: pricing is negotiated, and fees can exceed those of comparable merchant-of-record services. Small teams tend to be better served elsewhere.
label: negative

text: [FastSpring] Documentation for FastSpring's APIs is thin, and community support is small. Troubleshooting integrations mostly means waiting for tickets to be answered.
label: negative

text: [Chargebee] Chargebee gets expensive as you scale, since its plans are tied to revenue. Many teams report that the bill outgrows the value, especially once add-ons are needed.
label: negative

text: [Chargebee] Chargebee's configuration is heavy. Plans, add-ons and dunning rules take a lot of setup, and a small team can easily get lost in the options.
label: negative

text: [Chargebee] Chargebee does not process payments itself, so you still need a gateway and have to pay two vendors. For simple billing needs, that extra layer is an unnecessary cost.
label: negative

text: [Zuora] Zuora implementations are famously long and costly. Projects often need consultants and several months, which makes it an unrealistic pick for anyone below enterprise scale.
label: negative

text: [Zuora] Users describe Zuora's interface as clunky and slow. Even basic changes to a pricing plan can require expert help, which hurts agility.
label: negative

text: [Checkout.com] Checkout.com focuses on large merchants, and smaller businesses report slow onboarding and limited help. Pricing is custom, so it is difficult to evaluate without a sales call.
label: negative

text: [Checkout.com] Checkout.com's dashboard and reporting get mixed feedback, and some merchants say integration issues took too long to resolve. I would shortlist other providers first.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] If you need a merchant of record, Stripe is not the answer: you stay liable for sales tax and VAT. Pairing it with a separate tax service raises both cost and complexity.
label: negative

text: [Paddle] One downside of Paddle is its limited payment method coverage in some regions. Local options that buyers expect may be missing, which can lower checkout conversion.
label: negative

text: [Stripe] Stripe's fraud tool Radar sometimes blocks legitimate customers, and tuning the rules requires expertise. False declines quietly cost some merchants real revenue.
label: negative

text: [PayPal] PayPal's checkout often redirects buyers away from your site, which feels dated and can reduce trust. Its brand strength doesn't make up for the rough experience.
label: negative

text: [Adyen] Adyen's platform has a steep learning curve, and the dashboard exposes many options that overwhelm new users. It's more complicated than most small teams need.
label: negative

text: [Braintree] Braintree's pricing is not bad, but its limited coverage of local payment methods and aging SDKs make it a poor match for new, international products.
label: negative
